newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: New Malaysian unit trust taps into young savers.
newsitem.headline: New Malaysian unit trust taps into young savers.

text.p: A Malaysian unit trust fund being launched on Wednesday breaks new ground by targeting the country's youth and is the first government-managed fund open to all ethnic groups, analysts said.

The three billion ringgit Amanah Saham Wawasan 2020, or ASW 2020, being launched by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad will be open to all Malaysians aged between 12 and 29 years old. They make up about 40 percent of the population.
Previous government-managed unit trusts were restricted to Bumiputeras, or ethnic Malays.
In the breakdown, 51 percent of the fund will be set aside for Bumiputeras and the rest for non-Bumiputeras, who consist of Chinese, Indians and other ethnic groups.
It will invest in stocks and money market instruments and eventually in overseas markets.
"It crosses the barriers," said Razani Radzi of PB Securities research department. "I think that's positive. It makes things a lot more transparent and a lot more accountable."
The fund aims to promote savings by younger Malaysians and provide financing for infrastructure and privatised projects.
"It's extremely significant," said William Chan, an institutional dealer at Seagroatt and Campbell. "This money goes into the stock market and deepens it, but is also venture capital.

ASW 2020 carries not only Malaysia's hopes for elevating its nascent fund management industry but takes its very name from the political and social "Vision 2020" of evolving into an industrialised nation by that year.
By that time, Malaysia reckons some of ASW 2020's investors will be approaching retirement age, and the unit trust is also being marketed as a pension scheme.

The unit trust's entrance into an industry with assets of over 44 billion ringgit in Malaysia will also work to pull in funds that could otherwise add to Malaysia's overheated consumption, analysts said.

The government, concerned about an overheated economy that is now entering its ninth year of eight percent or better growth, has tried to brake consumption spending through financing restrictions and other policies.
"It (the fund) serves two purposes: to get funding and to siphon off money from people so consumption won't be so strong," said Rajeev Malik, an economist at Jardine Fleming.
Malaysia wants to increase its savings rate to 40 percent of gross domestic product by 2000, from the current 34.60 percent.
The introduction of this new fund is also another step for Malaysia to position itself as a rival financial services hub in the region, analysts said.
"I think it is very exciting for Malaysia," said Christopher Chong, head of economic research at Kay Hian James Capel. "It very much focuses Kuala Lumpur as a finance centre."
